meta.program: The Bench · Manager Monday · Anchor's Edge · Vanderbilt
meta.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; this session opens the February Retain, Grow, Move month on succession and internal mobility.
meta.roomSetup: Virtual, instructor led: camera on, deck link in chat, breakouts of 2 available. Learners follow on their own screens via the welcome-slide link or QR. Nothing typed into the deck is saved or sent.
meta.postSession: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the bench move on your card happen? How did the growth framing land? Who is on the pipeline for your own role now?' Count of opened bench conversations is the Level 3 metric for the month.

full.description: The full 45-minute virtual session: every interaction runs live, breakouts run in pairs, and the capstone gets read-alouds. The per-section minutes on each slide sum to 45 including transitions.

core.description: The 30-minute slot: agenda and core-idea slides pass in stride, breakouts become solo passes with chat share-outs, debriefs shrink to one voice. Never cut the section interactions or the capstone.

meta.framework: ATD facilitator-guide structure: per module SAY / DO / ASK (with anticipated responses) / DEBRIEF / TRANSITION, plus preparation checklists, materials, contingencies, and a tough-questions bank.
materials: Meeting platform with screen share and breakout rooms; deck link ready to paste in chat
Facilitator machine with the facilitator edition open; notifications off
Learners on their own devices with the learner link
Chat open for share-outs; the capstone copy button pastes there cleanly

weekBefore: Run the learner edition start to finish and do every interaction honestly; you will demo at least one live.
Read this month's theme page on the Anchor's Edge dashboard so the goal tie-in is fluent.
Send the invite with the learner link and one line on what to bring.
dayBefore: Test screen share with the facilitator edition; confirm the notes rail is readable.
Open the learner link on a second device; the QR must land there.
Run the section interactions once so you can drive them without reading.
thirtyMinBefore: Welcome slide up as people join; link pasted in chat.
Close every other tab; silence the machine.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: A manager says naming a bench will make people expect promotions
contingencies.then: Give the honest-language line: readiness and direction, never a guarantee. 'I want to grow you toward bigger work' promises development, and development is deliverable.

contingencies.if: Someone names a real colleague while describing their bench
contingencies.then: Protect them warmly and immediately: 'Hold that. Roles, never names.' Bench membership is sensitive people data; it never gets discussed by name on a group call.

toughQuestions.q: Won't a succession conversation make my best person start job hunting?
toughQuestions.a: The research runs the other way: people leave when growth is invisible, and a bench seat makes it visible. If the worry stays with you, the stay-interview practice lab attached to this month's LinkedIn Learning course, Retaining Your Best Talent, was built for exactly this.

toughQuestions.q: What if I build a bench and the role never opens?
toughQuestions.a: Then the person still got stretch work, new skills, and proof that someone invested in them, and the Transfer Portal gives those skills somewhere to go inside Vanderbilt. A bench that never gets promoted still retains and still grows.

toughQuestions.q: Do I need my own manager's approval to build a pipeline for my role?
toughQuestions.a: Loop them in, because a manager developing successors is good news upward. What needs no approval: growing skills on your team and being honest with people about direction. Start there.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Monday, 45 minutes on succession without the scare. Bring a quiet thought about one person you would trust with bigger work. You will never be asked to name them. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the bench move happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the move on your card happen? 2) How did the growth framing land? 3) Who is on your own role's pipeline now?

sections.title: Welcome / QR
sections.purpose: Get everyone into the deck on their own screen and set the tone: 45 minutes, live, hands on.
sections.say: Welcome to Manager Monday. Scan the code or click the link in chat so this session runs on your screen too. Forty-five minutes, one focus: Succession conversations that don't scare people.
facilitate: Slide up as people join; link pasted in chat every few minutes.
State the norm once: type into your own screen, nothing you enter is saved or sent.
sections.watchFor: People lurking without the deck open. The interactions only land if the deck is on their screen.
sections.transition: Before the topic, thirty seconds on why Vanderbilt is asking for this hour.

sections.title: Why we're here
sections.purpose: Anchor the session in the Chancellor's charge and name the goal this month serves, inside one minute.
sections.say: One sentence from the Chancellor sits over everything we do: Vanderbilt will define the great university of the 21st Century and be it. A university built to define the century cannot wobble every time a key person moves on; deep benches are Exceptional Core Operations in human form. This month serves Goal 1, Talent Marketplace & Transfer Portal.
facilitate: Read the mission line slowly, once; name the goal, once.
No discussion here; the whole slide is under a minute.
sections.transition: Here is what you will be able to do in 45 minutes.

sections.title: Objectives
sections.purpose: Set the contract for the session in under a minute.
sections.say: By the end of this session: reframe succession planning as growth planning for the people on the bench; open a succession conversation without triggering replacement fear; name the start of a successor pipeline for your own role. That is the whole contract.
facilitate: Read the three objectives briskly; do not elaborate yet.

sections.title: Agenda
sections.purpose: Show the path so the room can pace itself.
sections.say: Three stops: the bench is a gift, the fearless opening, your own pipeline. Each one has something to play with, so keep the deck open.
facilitate: Point once at each stop; ten seconds each.
sections.coreNote: Core: skip the read-through, gesture at the slide in passing.

sections.title: The bench is a gift
sections.purpose: Install the reframe: succession planning is growth planning for the people named to the bench.
sections.say: Succession is the word managers whisper, because everyone in earshot hears replacement. Here is the reframe this whole month stands on: a bench is a list of people someone is betting on, and a seat on it is a gift. Harvard Business Review looked across the succession research and found the same thing, that plans run as living development actually work, while the ones kept in a drawer for emergencies quietly fail. We whisper this word. We should be handing it over like good news.
facilitate: Read the concept card aloud once, slowly; it carries the reframe.
Show the In the room card and let it land, then open the discussion prompt: why do these plans stay secret? Take two or three voices.
Run the breakout: say the bench sentence out loud, gift or threat, 90 seconds each way.

ask.q: When you were first put on a bench or a plan yourself, how did you hear it?
expect: Stories of it landing as a vote of confidence
Stories of quiet panic about being managed out
Some were never told, and found out later
ask.respond: All three answers teach the same thing: the framing decided the feeling. That framing is yours to control for your team.

sections.debrief: The plan is the same document either way. The framing decides whether it retains someone or scares them.
sections.watchFor: Managers treating succession as a form for HR. Redirect to the person: what does the seat give them this quarter?
sections.transition: The reframe only survives contact if the opening lines are right. That is next.
sections.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for gift-or-threat votes in chat instead.

sections.title: The fearless opening
sections.purpose: Train ears to hear which openings land as investment, which trigger replacement fear, and which are too vague to land.
sections.say: Nobody remembers slide four of a succession conversation. They remember the first two sentences, and they decide in those two sentences whether this is a promotion track or a pink slip. So we are going to train on openings. Same news, three framings, and only one of them earns the conversation.
facilitate: Run Gift or threat? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round one, pause: ask who called it differently and why.
Run the breakout: say your own opening line, partner reports the first feeling it raises.

ask.q: Why does the compliance opening, the HR-needs-a-name one, do so much damage?
expect: It makes the person a box to fill
It suggests the decision already happened somewhere else
It attaches their role to someone else's name
ask.respond: Right. It contains no growth and no future for the listener. Every strong opening starts with the person, never the chart.

sections.debrief: Growth openings earn the conversation. Org-chart openings put fear in the room first, and vague warmth books nothing.
sections.watchFor: Managers drafting openings that promise a promotion. Growth language must stay honest: readiness and direction, never a guarantee.
sections.transition: You can open it for your team. Now the harder one: your own chair.
sections.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

sections.title: Your own pipeline
sections.purpose: Get every manager to start a skills-first, multi-person pipeline for their own role and say it out loud.
sections.say: Here is the move that separates managers who talk succession from managers who build it: naming a pipeline for your own role. It feels risky, and it reads as the opposite. A leader with a bench looks secure, and gets freed up for bigger work. Build it skills first, put more than one name on it, and tell the people you put there.
facilitate: Run Start your pipeline; two minutes to make both choices and run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: skills first, several people, growth that starts now.

ask.q: What stops managers from naming successors for their own role?
expect: Fear the person will expect a promotion
Nobody on the team feels ready
ask.respond: Name the flip: a role only you can do is a role you can never be promoted out of. The bench is your own mobility plan too.

sections.debrief: A secret bench grows nobody. Skills first, several names, and the growth conversation happens this quarter.
sections.watchFor: Managers picking one heir apparent. Push for two or three; a single name recreates the replacement drama on a new person.
sections.transition: Quick recap, then you build your own bench card.
sections.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.purpose: Land the one sentence the session exists to install.
sections.say: If you keep one sentence from today, this is it. Read it once, out loud: A bench is a gift to the person on it.
facilitate: Pause two beats after reading; the word animation carries it.
sections.coreNote: Core: pass through in stride; the sentence reads itself.

sections.title: Recap quiz
sections.purpose: Score the learning while it is fresh; wrong answers are teaching moments, not failures.
sections.say: Three questions, on your own screen. Answer honestly; the explanations are where the learning sticks.
facilitate: Give the room 90 seconds to run it individually.
Ask for a show of results in chat: how many got 3 of 3?
Read out the explanation for whichever question drew the most misses.
sections.watchFor: Rushing past the why lines. The explanations carry the teaching.
sections.transition: Now point it at your real week.

sections.title: Capstone commitment
sections.purpose: Convert the session into one named, dated action per person.
sections.say: Now make it real. One person whose growth this is about, role only, never a name. Pick the move, pick the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitate: Two quiet minutes; everyone builds their own card.
Invite two or three volunteers to read their card aloud or paste it in chat.
Remind: copy the card somewhere you will see it this week.
sections.watchFor: Vague entries. Nudge for a name-able situation and a real date.

sections.title: Closing
sections.purpose: End with the next step and where this thread continues.
sections.say: You leave with a reframe and one bench move on a card. Make it this week. Tomorrow's Take-Off Tuesday points the Talent Marketplace and the Transfer Portal at everyone's own career: planning your growth and your next internal move, on purpose. Thursday's Thrive Thursday teaches advocacy: the difference between a mentor who advises you and a sponsor who spends their credibility on you. Same week, one theme: retain, grow, move, without the fear. And if you want to go deeper on retention this month, the LinkedIn Learning course Retaining Your Best Talent by Roberta Matuson comes with a navigator-led stay-interview practice lab.
facilitate: Point at the next-step card; one sentence.
Name the rest of the week's rhythm: the other sessions echo this month's theme.
